Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-english-main-1-prompt-long-0110", "row_sha256": "cc37952eb87af126f732eda11c5409684207903fe4fa713a54f42578634defb3", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "
could you turn this into a clear prompt for a short ordinary field update, not a press release, about one fictional trail sign replacement at millstone preserve? it should read like a self-contained account from someone familiar with the site, with connected paragraphs and enough concrete detail to make the episode feel real. the update is about work already done, not a proposal or a general guide to trail maintenance. use the details below as the episode facts, and don't turn the prompt into the update itself.

the sign is at the junction of the Juniper Loop and the Stone Bridge spur, about 2.4 miles from the lower parking area. hikers reach it after the path crosses a shallow drainage and bends left beside a stand of alder. the preserve map calls the junction “Alder Bend,” but that name is not printed on the old sign, so don't suggest that it was. the old board was put up in 2011 and its lower-right corner split during the winter. an inspection on June 3 found that the split had reached one of the bolt holes. the lettering could still be read at close range, but the arrow to the spur was partly hidden behind a curled edge. that inspection prompted the replacement; it wasn't a report of a fallen tree or a change to either trail.

on June 12, a crew of three replaced the board. they carried the new panel in from the lower lot on foot, using the service path for the first mile and then the marked trail. the replacement is recycled plastic, 24 by 18 inches, mounted on the existing two cedar posts. both posts were checked before the new panel went up. one was firm, and the other needed a small wedge at its base; neither post was removed. they reused the stainless-steel bolts after cleaning them, and the crew packed out the cracked board and the old washers. don't say that the posts were replaced, that new footing was poured, or that the work involved a larger construction project. no power equipment was brought to the junction.

the face has the preserve's name at the top, then the Juniper Loop arrow pointing left and the Stone Bridge spur arrow pointing right. it gives the spur as 0.6 mile to the footbridge and identifies the loop as 3.1 miles back to the lower lot. those route names and distances were checked against the current paper map before the panel was mounted. the map itself wasn't revised as part of this job. there was no change to the trail alignment, and don't imply that the spur now reaches a different destination. the crew spent about forty minutes at the junction, including a brief pause while two hikers passed through. the trails stayed open, with no detour and no closure notice.

include one ordinary quote from the volunteer who helped carry the panel. what she actually said was, “I could read the old one if I stopped right beside it, but the curled corner made the spur arrow easy to miss.” report that as her observation, not as an official assessment or a claim that every hiker had the same experience. she was carrying the panel with the crew and did not install the bolts. don't add a name for her, since none is provided. it would be useful for the update to mention that the new panel's lettering is dark green on a pale background and that the distance figures are larger than on the old board, but don't claim a particular typeface, reflectivity, or nighttime visibility.

make the update have a natural opening that puts the reader at the junction and explains why the board was replaced, then move through the work and what is printed on the new panel. use several connected paragraphs instead of a list of disconnected facts. a numbered section could fit if it helps the update distinguish the installation details, but don't force a table or turn every detail into a separate heading. keep the tone plain and specific. include a clear final section, but don't add a recap that repeats the opening or an approval, recommendation, or claim that the work solved every wayfinding issue. spread the relevant facts through the update rather than loading them all into the first paragraph.

for the ending, retain the actual scope and conditions of the walk-through assessment, and don't broaden it into a general finding. the assessment was made on June 12 after installation. its exact wording is: “At the June 12 walk-through, lettering could be read from the approach in ordinary daylight, provided the reader was on the packed path and not behind the fern growth; this assessment covers the westbound approach only and does not establish visibility after dark or from the eastbound side.” put this in the final paragraph, with any distinct final information there rather than an invented summary. don't drop the date, the daylight condition, the packed-path condition, the fern-growth limitation, or either limit on the assessment's scope. the finished update should remain a single fictional episode, complete and self-contained, with no extra events added beyond these facts.", "output": "Write a self-contained, plainspoken field update about the completed replacement of a trail sign at Millstone Preserve. Treat it as one fictional episode, not a proposal, press release, general maintenance guide, or summary of a larger project. Use connected paragraphs, distribute the facts throughout, and include a clear final section. A numbered section may be used if it fits naturally, but do not force headings or a table. Do not add events, claims, recommendations, approvals, or conclusions beyond the facts below.

**Location and reason for replacement:** The sign stands at the junction of the Juniper Loop and the Stone Bridge spur, about 2.4 miles from the lower parking area. The approach crosses a shallow drainage and bends left beside a stand of alder. The preserve map calls the junction “Alder Bend,” though that name is not printed on the old sign. The old board, installed in 2011, had a split in its lower-right corner after the winter. A June 3 inspection found the split had reached a bolt hole. Its lettering remained readable at close range, but a curled edge partly concealed the spur arrow. This prompted the replacement; there was no report of a fallen tree or a trail change.

**Work completed:** On June 12, a three-person crew carried the new panel from the lower lot, following the service path for the first mile and then the marked trail. The recycled-plastic panel measures 24 by 18 inches and is mounted on the existing two cedar posts. The crew checked both posts: one was firm, and the other needed a small wedge at its base. Neither post was removed. The crew cleaned and reused the stainless-steel bolts, then packed out the cracked board and old washers. No power equipment was brought to the junction. Do not state that the posts were replaced, new footing was poured, or a larger construction project took place.

The new sign displays the preserve’s name, with the Juniper Loop arrow pointing left and the Stone Bridge spur arrow pointing right. It lists the spur as 0.6 mile to the footbridge and the loop as 3.1 miles back to the lower lot. The crew checked the route names and distances against the current paper map before mounting the panel; the map was not revised. Neither the trail alignment nor the spur’s destination changed. The crew spent about forty minutes at the junction, pausing briefly to let two hikers pass. Both trails remained open, with no detour or closure notice.

Include the volunteer’s ordinary, unattributed quote exactly: “I could read the old one if I stopped right beside it, but the curled corner made the spur arrow easy to miss.” Present it as her observation, not an official assessment or a claim about all hikers. She helped carry the panel but did not install the bolts; no name is provided. The new panel has dark green lettering on a pale background, and its distance figures are larger than those on the old board. Do not specify a typeface, reflectivity, or nighttime visibility.

End with the walk-through assessment in the final paragraph, preserving its exact wording and limits: “At the June 12 walk-through, lettering could be read from the approach in ordinary daylight, provided the reader was on the packed path and not behind the fern growth; this assessment covers the westbound approach only and does not establish visibility after dark or from the eastbound side.” Keep the date, daylight and packed-path conditions, fern-growth limitation, and both limits on scope. Do not broaden the assessment or append an invented summary."}]
